props.title: Tales of Terror
props.initialSlug: Vincent Price stars in three Poe horror tales

sections.content: Tales of Terror (1962) stands as a pivotal anthology horror film in Roger Corman's celebrated Edgar Allan Poe cycle. Vincent Price delivers three distinct performances across adaptations of "Morella," "The Black Cat" (combined with "The Cask of Amontillado"), and "The Facts in the Case of M. Valdemar." This film bridges the gap between the gothic horror traditions established in House of Usher (1960) and the more experimental Poe adaptations like The Masque of the Red Death (1964). The film's structure influenced later horror anthologies like Creepshow (1982) and Trilogy of Terror (1975).

sections.content: The middle segment, combining "The Black Cat" and "The Cask of Amontillado," showcases Corman's ability to blend horror with dark comedy. Peter Lorre and Vincent Price's wine-tasting competition provides genuinely funny moments before descending into murderous revenge. This approach influenced later horror-comedy hybrids like An American Werewolf in London (1981) and Evil Dead II (1987), proving horror and humor could effectively coexist.

Richard Matheson's screenplay adaptations demonstrate how to successfully modernize Poe's themes while maintaining their gothic essence. His work here preceded his influential adaptations for The Last Man on Earth (1964) and The Legend of Hell House (1973), establishing a template for literary horror adaptations that continues through films like The Woman in Black (2012). movies.title: Masque of the Red Death
movies.slug: Price stars in this psychedelic Poe adaptation about a sadistic prince hiding from a plague

sections.content: Price's versatility across the three segments showcases why he became horror's preeminent star of the 1960s. His bereaved father in "Morella," scheming wine connoisseur in "The Black Cat," and mesmerized victim in "Valdemar" display remarkable range. This multi-role approach influenced later anthology performances like Dead of Night (1945) and inspired Price's subsequent work in The Abominable Dr. Phibes (1971).
